strengths: The problem is well motivated: predicting human response times under changing feedback is relevant to cognitive modeling and adaptive interfaces. Combining task-trained representations with an evidence-accumulation controller is a plausible contribution.

The study provides 21,157 trials from 36 retained participants across four feedback conditions and two days, including choices, response times, and attention/anxiety ratings. This is a useful empirical resource.

Evaluation includes individual, group, pooled, and leave-one-participant-out settings. The hybrid achieves consistently lower aggregate MAPE than the pure-DRL comparator; for example, Figure 6e reports 0.2905 versus 0.3037 under LOPO.
The overall pipeline is understandable, and the manuscript provides links to data and code, supporting further examination and reproduction.
weaknesses: The central cognitive interpretation is insufficiently supported. The purported drift-diffusion component constructs an assumed sigmoid trajectory from 0.5 to an SVC probability, with duration determined by SVR (Methods, p. 12). No corresponding stochastic drift/diffusion dynamics or validation against choice and response-time distributions is provided. Moreover, a reward based on terminal response-time error cannot uniquely identify intermediate evidence trajectories. Figure 7 therefore visualizes the model's assumptions and learned behavior without establishing that it recovers human cognitive mechanisms.

The learned corrections are not convincingly isolated as effects of time pressure. The manuscript does not clearly identify which pressure-free observations train the claimed baseline, and the controller can compensate for ordinary baseline prediction errors. Nonzero 'time pressure effect' trajectories in the no-pressure group (Figure 7a) illustrate this ambiguity. Cue-removal controls, an elapsed-time/presence baseline, and evaluation under altered cue timing would help establish whether fine-grained stimulus information explains the gains.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution. The pure-DRL baseline differs in visual representation, action scaling, and episode structure; it processes 25 × 2048 Inception features for each video. Consequently, the reported training-time advantage cannot be attributed specifically to incorporating an accumulation model. Comparisons with direct supervised response-time predictors and established covariate-dependent accumulation models, together with matched ablations, are needed to substantiate the benefit over prior approaches.

The predictive improvements over pure DRL are modest and lack uncertainty estimates: pooled MAPE is 0.2999 versus 0.3034, and individual-level MAPE is 0.2667 versus 0.2713. Participant-level paired confidence intervals and clearly documented repeated runs would establish their reliability. LOPO is valuable, but chronological plots of held-out participants do not establish prospective prediction or generalization to unseen feedback schedules.

The behavioral conclusions need more careful statistical support. Three participants are excluded as extreme outliers without operational criteria, leaving only seven participants in the random condition. Between-group post hoc comparisons are described as paired t-tests despite independent group assignment, requiring clarification or reanalysis. The absence of a significant anxiety group effect also limits interpreting the manipulation specifically as psychological stress.

Important reproduction details remain unspecified in the manuscript, including the exact sigmoid and accumulation-update equations, the value of λ, adaptive-feedback thresholds, and handling of the ten-second response-time limit. The evaluation should also explicitly document whether all human-data-dependent SVC/SVR fitting occurs within each outer training split. These omissions impede verification despite the provided repository links.
